lessons: Lead hooks with bold, concrete historical or scientific comparisons (e.g., 'older than the United States' achieved 1.85 retention at 10% and over 1.0 at the end).

Avoid verbatim repetition of the video title or hook in the first line; repeating the question causes massive immediate drop-offs (e.g., repeating the potato sprouting question caused a 31.9% drop at 9%).
Eliminate filler transition statements like 'They are not just there to look cool' or 'They look like similar fruits', which trigger 30%+ drop rates around 10-14% into the video.
Do not pause for audience countdowns or 'Pause and guess' prompts, as these directly cause steep mid-video viewer drops (e.g., up to 15.2% lost during countdowns in the foil and syrup videos).

Present active scientific comparisons and counter-intuitive facts (e.g., Red tuna vs White cod meat held 65.8% retention at 50%), rather than standard anatomical explanations which suffer heavy retention decay (e.g., leg asleep and funny bone dropped to under 10% at the end).
worst_moment_types: Verbatim repetition of the hook question immediately after the opening
Generic filler setup lines ('They look like similar fruits', 'They are not just there to look cool')
Interactive prompts and countdown pauses ('Pause and guess... three, two, one')
Stating obvious common knowledge before delivering the scientific cause
best_hook_types: Surprising, concrete comparative statements ('older than the United States')
Challenging scientific consensus or major space discoveries ('Scientists missed an outer Kuiper belt')
Intriguing mystery claims about high-profile topics ('Most James Webb images hold secrets')
Direct side-by-side visual/physical contradictions ('tuna steak looks like deep red beef, while a cod fillet is bright white')
